rice_healthy.description: Foliage shows vibrant linear green leaves with erect flag leaf positioning, uniform vein architecture, and complete absence of water-soaked streaks, necrotic lesions, or fungal fruiting structures.
symptoms: Smooth, bright green linear leaf blades with clean margins
Robust tillering with strong culms and intact flag leaves
No discoloration, chlorosis, or necrotic spotting along the leaf edges
causes: Proper water level management (saturated during transplanting, controlled flooding 2-5 cm during tillering)
Optimum seedling density and weed-free bund management

organic: Incorporate green manure (such as Sesbania or Azolla) to build native soil microbiological suppressiveness
Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.5%) suspension as a prophylactic phyllosphere protectant
chemical: No chemical pesticides or bactericides necessary for healthy stands

fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in split doses: 50% basal at transplanting, 25% at active tillering, and 25% at panicle initiation
Ensure adequate muriate of potash (MOP); potassium strengthens culms and promotes silica cell deposition in epidermis
Supplement with zinc sulfate (25 kg/ha) if soils show historical zinc deficiency (khaira condition)
irrigation: Practice Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) to oxygenate the root zone and prevent anaerobic sulfide accumulation
Maintain a consistent 3-5 cm water layer from panicle initiation through flowering, draining 10 days before harvest
prevention: Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride or hot water (52-54°C for 10 min) prior to nursery nursery sowing
Maintain 20 cm x 15 cm plant spacing to optimize microclimate ventilation and sunlight interception
recovery_tips: Perform periodic field perimeter weed clearance to eliminate alternate graminaceous hosts
Scout lower leaf sheaths weekly during the active tillering and boot leaf stages

rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.description: One of the most destructive rice diseases worldwide. Symptoms appear as water-soaked lesions on leaf margins that rapidly enlarge, turn yellowish-white, and develop wavy margins running lengthwise along leaf veins. Bacterial oozing beads may appear in morning dew.
symptoms: Water-soaked to yellowish-green translucent streaks starting at leaf tips and margins
Lesions advance into grayish-white necrotic blighted ribbons with characteristic wavy borders
Milky bacterial exudate droplets visible on lesions in early morning, drying into yellow crusty beads
Systemic kresek phase causing severe seedling wilting and death
causes: High humidity (> 70%) combined with warm temperatures (25-34°C)
Excessive, un-split nitrogen fertilization causing succulent leaf tissues
Typhoons, driving rain, or windstorms creating micro-wounds for bacterial entry
Deep standing irrigation water facilitating horizontal bacterial dispersal

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; localized tip lesions on lower outer leaves
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; wavy necrotic ribbons extending along outer 1/3 of leaf blade
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; widespread blighting of upper canopy and flag leaves, severe wilting (kresek)

organic: Spray plant extracts such as neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or garlic extract to suppress bacterial proliferation
Foliar spray with Pseudomonas fluorescens (2.5 kg/ha) or Bacillus subtilis bioprotectants
chemical: Spray Streptomycin sulfate + Tetracycline hydrochloride (Plantomycin / Agrimycin 100-150 g/ha) mixed with Copper oxychloride (500 g/ha)
Apply Bismerthiazol or Thiodiazole copper as per local agricultural regulatory guidelines
Repeat application after 10-12 days if rainy conditions persist

fertilizer: Immediately suspend all top-dressed nitrogenous fertilizers until the disease is arrested
Apply supplemental potassium (MOP at 25-30 kg/ha) to enhance epidermal cell wall lignification and plant defenses
Foliar spray 1% potassium nitrate (KNO3) to promote physiological recovery
irrigation: Drain standing field water immediately to 1 cm or allow field to dry for 3-4 days until soil cracks slightly
Never allow irrigation water to flow from infected paddies directly into healthy adjacent plots (stop field-to-field overflow)
Avoid irrigating during midday or turbulent rainy spells
prevention: Cultivate certified resistant cultivars containing Xa4, xa5, Xa21 resistance genes
Perform seed soaking in streptocycline solution (100 ppm) for 8 hours prior to nursery germination
Avoid root clipping or mechanical damage to seedlings during transplanting
Eradicate wild weed grass hosts (such as Leersia oryzoides and Cyperus species) from irrigation channels
recovery_tips: Plow under infected stubble immediately after harvest to accelerate bacterial decomposition
Allow paddies to undergo summer fallowing and solarization before the subsequent cropping season

rice_brown_spot.description: Historically linked to severe yield losses, brown spot is a fungal disease often associated with nutrient-deficient or poor soil conditions. Lesions are oval, dark brown with a gray/whitish center, resembling sesame seeds scattered on the foliage and grains.
symptoms: Small circular to oval brown spots with a distinct yellow halo across leaf blades
Fully developed spots are shaped like sesame seeds with grayish-white centers and dark brown margins
Spots coalesce into large irregular patches causing entire leaves to yellow and dry up prematurely
Infected spikelets show dark brown to black glume discoloration resulting in unfilled, chalky grains
causes: Severe soil nutrient deficiency (especially silicon, potassium, nitrogen, and manganese)
Unbalanced sandy soils or acid-sulfate soils with low organic matter
Prolonged leaf wetness (> 16 hours) and high relative humidity (85-95%) at 20-30°C
Drought stress or intermittent water deficit

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; small scattered oval spots on lower leaves only
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; dense spotting across middle canopy with yellow halos merging
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; total foliar blighting, panicle discoloration, and glume staining

organic: Foliar spray with neem oil (3 ml/L) or datura leaf extract at the onset of lesions
Apply bio-fungicides containing Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis to colonize lesion margins
chemical: Spray systemic fungicides: Propiconazole 25% EC (1 ml/L), Hexaconazole 5% EC (2 ml/L), or Tebuconazole
Protectant sprays of Mancozeb 75% WP (2 g/L) or Carbendazim (1 g/L)
Apply at active tillering and repeat at panicle emergence (booting stage)

fertilizer: Ameliorate soil nutritional stress: apply balanced NPK supplemented with farmyard manure (FYM) or vermicompost
Apply calcium silicate slag or potassium silicate (100-200 kg/ha) to replenish plant silicon levels
Correct manganese and zinc deficiencies via foliar sprays of 0.5% MnSO4 and 0.5% ZnSO4
irrigation: Maintain continuous shallow flooding (2-4 cm) during tillering and panicle development to eliminate drought stress
Avoid severe soil drying cycles in light-textured soils prone to brown spot development
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed; hot water treatment at 53-54°C for 10-12 minutes
Seed dressing with Carbendazim or Thiram at 2 g/kg of seed before sowing
Conduct soil testing before season planting to correct macro and micronutrient deficiencies
recovery_tips: Burn or compost infected crop residues with urea to accelerate fungal perithecial breakdown
Rotate with leguminous green manure crops to restore organic matter and soil health

rice_leaf_smut.description: Leaf smut is a widespread fungal disease characterized by small, slightly raised, angular black spots (sori) on both surfaces of the leaf blade. As the disease advances, leaves turn yellow from the tip, turn brown, and wither prematurely.
symptoms: Small, slightly raised, angular black spots (1-3 mm) scattered across the leaf blade
Spots appear on both sides of the leaf, often bounded by small veins
Surrounding leaf tissue turns chlorotic yellow, leading to premature senescence of older leaves
Teliospores form dark crusty masses under the leaf epidermis
causes: Late cropping season maturity accompanied by heavy dew and warm temperatures (28-32°C)
Excessive nitrogen application late in the crop cycle
High plant density and sheltered microclimates with stagnant air

severity_rules.mild: < 10% coverage; sparse black sori on lower senescing leaves
severity_rules.moderate: 10% - 30% coverage; numerous black crusty spots with localized yellowing
severity_rules.severe: > 30% coverage; dense black pustules over entire blade with complete leaf desiccation

organic: Spray fermented buttermilk extract (5%) or wood ash tea to disrupt fungal spore viability
Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/L) to suppress epiphytic fungal development
chemical: Foliar spray with Mancozeb 75% WP (2 g/L) or Copper oxychloride 50% WP (2.5 g/L)
For severe outbreaks, apply systemic triazoles such as Propiconazole (1 ml/L) or Tebuconazole (1 ml/L)
Spray twice at 10-day intervals during late vegetative to heading stage

fertilizer: Avoid late-season top dressing of nitrogen fertilizer after heading
Balance potassium application (60 kg K2O/ha) to reinforce leaf structural integrity
Ensure adequate phosphorus availability during initial root establishment
irrigation: Avoid excessive ponding of water in late reproductive phases; implement alternate shallow wetting
Ensure proper drainage channels to prevent stagnant, humid micro-climates
prevention: Select varieties adapted with tolerance to late-season fungal foliar pathogens
Follow optimal seedling spacing (minimum 20 cm x 15 cm) to promote air circulation
Rogue out and destroy early infected leaves in seed multiplication plots
recovery_tips: Deeply plow stubble post-harvest to bury fungal teliospores beneath the microbial decomposition zone
Maintain clean bunds and eliminate wild rice volunteers
